entities.summary:
The Wall Street Journal, launched on July 8, 1889, by Charles Dow, Edward Jones, and Charles Bergstresser, swiftly became the definitive chronicle of American and global financial markets. Originating from Dow Jones & Company, it established the benchmark for business journalism, profoundly influencing investment decisions, corporate strategy, and public discourse on capitalism and economic policy worldwide for over a century. Its distinctive, often conservative, editorial voice and rigorous financial reporting have solidified its position as an indispensable authority on economic affairs, shaping the understanding of market dynamics from its lower Manhattan origins to a global audience.

Initially focusing on stock market news and the proprietary Dow Jones Industrial Average (established 1896), The Wall Street Journal rapidly expanded beyond mere listings to offer in-depth analytical pieces and pioneering investigative journalism. Notable achievements include its incisive coverage of the 1929 stock market crash, its critical reporting on the Enron scandal in the early 2000s, and its comprehensive chronicles of the 2008 financial crisis, earning numerous Pulitzer Prizes across various categories. The paper's acquisition by Rupert Murdoch's News Corp in 2007 marked a significant shift, bringing new resources and editorial scrutiny, while its commitment to data-driven reporting and global economic trends continued unabated.

Its consistent, high-quality coverage and editorial stance significantly contributed to the understanding and evolution of modern capitalism.
